1.7 years ago in /v/guns I posted about renting the Chiappa Rhino 200D snub-nose revolver from my local gun range.

Time has erased all the images I uploaded, including the one of the 6" variant of the Rhino that I linked to at the end when I said

I'm also loving the aesthetic of their 6" Rhino, though my local range didn't have one of those for rent... I'm probably going to get one.

But that's OK, because I finally got one! Along with a classic cowboy-leather-brown OWB leather holster

Pictures

  1. Holstered
  2. Unholstered
  3. Lying Flat
  4. Looking down the Barrel
  5. At the Range

Concerns

There were two things that I was a little worried about after renting the 200D (double-action-only) snub-nose Rhino:

Trigger Pull

In the double-action-only Rhino, there was no perceptible break in the trigger on the pull before it fired - it was smooth all the way back. Normally in a

revolver I could pull the trigger back until I felt the cylinder slide into position and the hammer release be in position, and then know that the next bit

of pressure would actually fire it - not so with the 200D.

When I saw a bunch of the DS Rhino models (meaning double action or single action), I was worried that they'd behave the same way. Luckily, this is not the

case - it's easy to feel when the cylinder is positioned and the gun will fire, just like any other revolver.

Decocking

Obviously there's no decocking a double-action-only revolver because there's no cocking it, either. Some people online said/worried that the DS Rhinos

weren't decockable. They are. The only weird thing is that the exposed hammer is actually a hammer lever, and rests in the "up" position even when cocked -

but if you pull it back, pull the trigger, and slowly release it, you can decock the revolver just like any other.

I guess it's a feature that there's no external hammer movement, meaning nothing can block it or get caught on it - once the Rhino's cocked, the hammer has a

clear shot to fire no matter what happens outside the frame.

Performance

It's perfect.

The action is buttery. The metal is matte-glossy and silky. The sights are fiber-optic, bright, and were dead-on from the factory (but if they hadn't been,

the rear sights are left-right and up-down adjustable with just a screwdriver). The grip is firm but also doesn't even feel like it's there. It's got a top

and bottom rail. The bottom-firing setup does perceptibly direct recoil more back than up, reducing muzzle flip.

So far, I've shot a wide variety of .38 special and .357 range ammo through it, in addition to some more "special" .357 rounds:

  1. Hornady LeverRevolution .357 Magnum (kicked like you wouldn't believe -

actually hurt after just one cylinder!) 2. HSM "Bear Load" 180 grain hardened lead .357 Magnum (kicked like you'd expect - just another magnum load) 3. Sig Sauer V-Crown Elite .357 Magnum (personal defense round. Unremarkable)

The bottom barrel combined with the length (6 inches) and weight make the hardest part of shooting .38 special not the recoil or muzzle flip, but holding the

gun in the air!

This was all at an indoor 25 yard range. If I'm feeling ridiculous, next time I'm at an outdoor range I'll mount a scope on the top rail and see how far out

I can maintain accuracy with the Hornady LeverRevolution .357s.

The only "trick" is that at close ranges (which really everything up to 25 yards was), the barrel being so much lower than the sights matters. So, instead of

sighting normally, line the front red dot up on the line "above" the top of the two green dots - so it sticks up like a rhino horn. Then, at close ranges,

it's dead-on to where I can pick a bullet-hole-sized feature on the target and put a bullet right in it.

10/10 would recommend.
